{{Short description|Creation of designs for the manufacturing of woven, knitted or printed fabrics}}
'''Textile design''', also known as '''textile geometry''', is the creative and technical process by which thread or [[yarn]] fibers are interlaced to form a piece of [[Textile|cloth]] or [[Textile|fabric]], which is subsequently printed upon or otherwise adorned.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Introduction|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref> Textile design is further broken down into three major disciplines: printed textile design, woven textile design, and mixed media textile design. Each uses different methods to produce a fabric for variable uses and markets. Textile design as an industry is involved in other disciplines such as [[fashion]], [[interior design]], and [[fine art]]s.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Briggs-Goode, A. (Amanda)|title=Printed textile design|isbn=978-1-78067-403-2|location=London|chapter=Introduction|oclc=898176484}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Russell |first=Alex|title=The Fundamentals of Printed Textile Design|year=2016|isbn=978-1-4742-1853-5|location=[London] |publisher=Bloomsbury |chapter=Introduction|oclc=1053941237}}</ref>[[File:Morris and Co Dove and Rose point paper.jpg|thumb|200px|Point paper for ''Dove and Rose'' woven [[double cloth]] by [[William Morris]], 1879]]

== Overview ==
Articles produced using textile design include [[clothing]], [[carpet]]s, [[Drapery|drapes]], and [[towel]]s.<ref name="Collier, Bide and Tortora">{{cite book |last1=Collier |first1=Billie J. |last2=Bide |first2=Martin J. |last3=Tortora |first3=Phyllis G.|title=Understanding of Textiles |url= |publisher=Pearson Prentice Hall |year=2009|location=Upper Saddle River, New Jersey |edition=7th |isbn=978-0-13-118770-2 |oclc=212376154}}</ref> Textile design requires an understanding of the technical aspects of [[textile manufacturing|the production process]], as well as the properties of numerous [[fiber]]s, [[yarn]]s, and [[dye]]s.<ref name="Gale">{{cite book |last1=Gale |first1=Colin |last2=Kaur |first2=Jasbir |date=2002 |title=The Textile Book |url= |location=Oxford |publisher=Berg |page=37 |isbn=1-85973-512-6 |oclc=48516971}}</ref>

== Textile design disciplines ==

=== Printed textile design ===
[[File:Textile,_Strawberry_Thief,_designed_1883,_printed_ca._1934_(CH_18340065).jpg|thumb|Printed textile design: [[William Morris]], [[Strawberry Thief (William Morris)|Strawberry Thief]], 1883<ref>{{Cite book|last=Parry |first=Linda |title=William Morris Textiles|date=1983 |location=New York |publisher=Viking Press|isbn=0-670-77075-2|oclc=8221337}}</ref>]]
Printed textile designs are created by using various printing techniques on fabric, cloth, and other materials. Printed textile designers are mainly involved in designing patterns for home interior products like carpets, wallpapers, and ceramics. They also work in the [[Fashion industry|fashion and clothing industries]], the [[Pulp and paper industry|paper industry]], and in designing stationery and [[Gift wrapping|gift wrap]].<ref>{{Citation|title=The framework|date=2011|url=https://www.bloomsburyappliedvisualarts.com/encyclopedia-chapter?docid=b-9781474218535&tocid=b-9781474218535-chapter1|work=The Fundamentals of Printed Textile Design|pages=8–43|publisher=AVA Publishing SA Distributed by Thames & Hudson (ex-North America) Distributed in the USA & Canada by: English Language Support Office|language=en|doi=10.5040/9781474218535.ch-001|isbn=978-1-4742-1853-5|access-date=2020-04-17|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

There are numerous established printed styles and designs that can be broken down into four major categories: floral, geometric, world cultures, and conversational.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last=Briggs-Goode |first=Amanda |title=Printed Textile Design |isbn=978-1-78067-403-2 |location=London |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Design in Context |oclc=898176484}}</ref> [[Floral design]]s include flowers, plants, or other botanical elements. [[Geometric design]]s feature elements, both inorganic and [[Abstract art|abstract]], such as [[tessellation]]s. World culture designs may be traced to a specific geographic, ethnic, or anthropological source. Finally, conversational designs are designs that fit less easily into the other categories; they may be described as presenting "imagery that references popular icons of a particular period or season, or which is unique and challenges our perceptions in some way."<ref name=":22" /> Each category contains subcategories, which include more specific individual styles and designs.<ref name=":22" />

Moreover, different fabrics, like [[silk]] and [[wool]], require different types of dye. Other protein-based fabrics require acidic dyes, whereas [[Synthetic fiber|synthetic fabrics]] require specialized [[disperse dye|dispersed dye]]s.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-78539-200-9 |location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Screen-printed textile designs |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

The advent of [[computer-aided design]] [[software]], such as [[Adobe Photoshop]] and [[Adobe Illustrator|Illustrator]], has allowed each discipline of textile design to evolve and innovate new practices and processes but has most influenced the production of printed textile designs.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London|chapter=Introduction|oclc=866622297}}</ref> Digital tools have influenced the process of creating repeating patterns or motifs, or repeats. Repeats are used to create patterns both visible and invisible to the eye: geometric patterns are intended to depict clear, intentional patterns, whereas floral or organic designs are intended to create unbroken repeats that are ideally undetectable. Digital tools have also aided in making patterns by decreasing the amount of an effect known as "tracking", in which the eye is inadvertently drawn to parts of textiles that expose the discontinuity of the textile and reveal its pattern.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Patterns and Repeats|oclc=866622297}}</ref> These tools, alongside the innovation of digital [[inkjet printing]], have allowed the textile printing process to become faster, more [[scalable]], and more [[sustainable]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Technology for Digital Textile Printing|oclc=866622297}}</ref>

=== Woven textile design ===
Woven textile design originates from the practice of [[weaving]], which produces fabric by interlacing a vertical yarn ([[Warp and weft|warp]]) and a horizontal yarn ([[Warp and weft|weft]]), most often at right angles.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Britannica Concise Encyclopedia |date=2006|publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica|isbn=978-1-84972-210-0|location=Chicago|chapter=Weaving|oclc=436847805}}</ref> Woven textile designs are created by various types of [[loom]]s and are now predominantly produced using a mechanized or computerized [[Jacquard machine|jacquard loom]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Hand Woven Textile Designs|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>[[File:Philbrook_-_Navajo_Satteldecke.jpg|thumb|Woven textile design: A woven [[Navajo]] [[saddle blanket]] from the [[Philbrook Museum of Art|Philbrook Museum]] in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma|Tulsa]], [[Oklahoma]]]]Designs within the context of weaving are created using various types of yarns, using variance in texture, size, and color to construct a stylized patterned or [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] fabric. There is a large range of yarn types available to the designer, including but not limited to [[cotton]], [[twill]], [[linen]], and synthetic fibers. To produce the woven fabric, the designer first delineates and visualizes the sequence of threading, which is traditionally drawn out on graph paper known as point paper.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rothstein |first=Natalie |date=1994 |title=The Victoria and Albert Museum's Textile Collection: Woven Textile Design in Britain 1750 to 1850 |url= |location=New York |publisher=Canopy Books |page= |isbn=9781558598508 |oclc=31203715}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Preparation for Design|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref>

The designer also will choose a weave structure that governs the aesthetic design that will be produced. The most common process is a [[plain weave]], in which the yarns interlace in an alternating, tight formation, producing a strong and flexible multi-use fabric. [[Twill]] weaves, which are also common, alternatively use diagonal lines created by floating the warp or the weft to the left or the right.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Twill Weaves|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref> This process creates a softer fabric favored by designers in the fashion and clothing design industries. Common, recognizable twill styles include patterns like [[Houndstooth]] or [[Herringbone (cloth)|Herringbone]].<ref name=":0" />

Beyond weave structure, [[color]] is another dominant aspect in woven textile design. Typically, designers choose two or more contrasting colors that will be woven into patterns based on a chosen threading sequence. Color is also dependent on the size of the yarn: fine yarns will produce a fabric that may change colors when it receives light from different angles, whereas larger yarns will generally produce a more [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] surface.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Colour and Weave|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref>

=== Mixed media textile design ===
[[File:Kazakh_rug_chain_stitch_embroidery.jpg|thumb|Mixed media textile design: An embroidered [[Kazakhs|Kazakh]], chain stitched rug]]
Mixed media textile designs are produced using [[embroidery]] or other various fabric manipulation processes such as [[pleat]]ing, [[appliqué]], [[quilting]], and [[laser cutting]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Mixed media textile design|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

Embroidery is traditionally performed by hand, applying myriad stitches of thread to construct designs and patterns on the textile surface. Similar to printed textile design, embroidery affords the designer artistic and aesthetic control. Typical stitches include but are not limited to the [[Cross-stitch|cross stitch]], the [[chain stitch]], and [[couching]]. Although industrial and [[Machine embroidery|mechanized embroidery]] has become the standard, hand stitching still remains a fixture for fine arts textiles.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Embroidered Textile Design|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

[[Quilting]] is traditionally used to enhance the insulation and warmth of a textile. It also provides the designer with the opportunity to apply aesthetic properties. Most commonly, [[quilt]]s feature geometric and [[collage]] designs formed from various textiles of different textures and colors. Quilting also frequently employs the use of recycled scrap or [[heirloom]] fabrics.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Fabric Manipulation|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref> Quilts are also often used as a medium for an artist to depict a personal or communal narrative: for example, the [[Hmong people]] have a tradition of creating story quilts or cloths illustrating their experiences with [[immigration]] to the [[United States]] from [[East Asia|Eastern]] and [[Southeast Asia|South-eastern Asia]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.wisc.edu/stitched-tapestry-of-hmong-history-unveiled-at-multicultural-center/|title=Stitched tapestry of Hmong history unveiled at Multicultural Center|last=Gjerde|first=Hearther|date=October 27, 2008|website=University of Wisconsin-Madison}}</ref>

== Environmental impact ==
The practice and industry of textile design present [[environmental concerns]]. From the production of cloth from raw material to dyeing and finishing, and the ultimate disposal of products, each step of the process produces environmental impacts. They have been further exacerbated with the emergence of [[fast fashion]] and other modern industrial practices.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Environmental Concerns|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

Predominantly, these environmental impacts stem from the heavy use of hazardous chemicals involved in the textile creation process which must be properly disposed of. Other considerations involve the amount of waste created by the disposal of textile design products and the reclamation and reuse of [[Recycling|recyclable]] textiles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Calamari|first1=Sage|last2=Hyllegard|first2=Karen H.|date=2016-07-07|title=An exploration of designers' perspectives on human health and environmental impacts of interior textiles|journal=Textiles and Clothing Sustainability|volume=2|issue=1|pages=9|doi=10.1186/s40689-016-0020-7|issn=2197-9936|doi-access=free}}</ref> The [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] reported that over 15 million tons of textile waste is created annually. This consists of some 5% of all [[Municipal solid waste|municipal waste]] generated. Only 15% of that waste is recovered and reused.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/2013_advncng_smm_rpt.pdf|title=Advancing Sustainable Materials Management: Facts and Figures 2013|website=United States Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref>

The existence and awareness of the negative environmental impacts of textile production has resulted in the emergence new technologies and practices. Textile designs involving the use of synthetic dyes and materials can result in harmful effects on the environment. This has caused a shift towards using natural dyes or materials and research towards other mediums that result in less harm to the environment. This research includes testing new ways to collect [[natural resource]]s and how these natural resources work with other materials.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2020-02-01|title=The education of art culture at Sultanate of Oman through the multidisciplinary integration between graphic design and eco-friendly textile printing. Part 1: Standardization of extraction and dyeing with natural wastes products|journal=Energy Reports|language=en|volume=6|pages=933–939|doi=10.1016/j.egyr.2019.12.020|issn=2352-4847|doi-access=free|last1=Mansour |first1=H. |last2=Hilal |first2=N. |last3=Alhajri |first3=S. |last4=Al-Yahyai |first4=F. |last5=Al-Amri |first5=M. |bibcode=2020EnRep...6..933M |hdl=10419/243845 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

[[Electronic textile]]s involve items of clothing with electronic devices or technology woven into the fabric, such as heaters, lights, or sensors. These textiles can potentially have additional harmful environmental effects, such as producing [[electronic waste]]. Because of this, these textiles are often made by manufacturers with sustainability in mind.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Köhler|first=Andreas R.|date=2013-10-01|title=Challenges for eco-design of emerging technologies: The case of electronic textiles|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261306913003270|journal=Materials & Design|language=en|volume=51|pages=51–60|doi=10.1016/j.matdes.2013.04.012|issn=0261-3069|url-access=subscription}}</ref> These new approaches to textile design attempt to lessen the negative environmental impact of these textiles.

These concerns have led to the birth of [[Sustainability|sustainable]] textile design movements and the practice of [[ecological design]] within the field. For instance, London's [[Royal Society of Arts|Royal Society of the Arts]] hosts design competitions that compel all entrants to center their design and manufacturing methods around sustainable practices and materials.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Textile design, the environment, and science|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

== Textile design in different cultures ==
[[File:African Textile Design Pattern.jpg|thumb|Strip-woven textile design: African fabric]]
Textile patterns, designs, weaving methods, and cultural significance vary across the world. African countries use textiles as a form of cultural expression and way of life. They use textiles to liven up the interior of a space or accentuate and decorate the body of an individual. The textile designs of African cultures involve the process of strip-woven fibers that can repeat a pattern or vary from strip to strip.<ref>{{Cite book|last=LaGamma|first=Alisa|title=The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End.|publisher=Metropolitan Museum of Art|year=2009|isbn=9780300149623|location=New York|pages=88–99}}</ref>

== History ==
The history of textile design dates back thousands of years. Due to the decomposition of textile fibers, early examples of textile design are rare. However, some of the oldest known and preserved examples of textiles were discovered in the form of [[Fishing net|nets]] and [[Basket weaving|basketry]], dating from [[Neolithic]] cultures in 5000 BCE. When [[Trade|trade networks]] formed in European countries, textiles like [[silk]], [[wool]], [[cotton]], and [[Flax|flax fibers]] became valuable commodities. Many early cultures including [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]], Chinese, African, and [[Peru]]vian practiced early weaving techniques. One of the oldest examples of textile design was found in an ancient [[Siberia]]n tomb in 1947. The tomb was said to be that of a prince aging back to 464 AD, making the tomb and all of its contents over 2,500 years old. The rug, known as the [[Pazyryk rug]], was preserved inside ice and is detailed with elaborate designs of deer and men riding on horseback. The designs are similar to present-day [[Anatolian rug|Anatolian]] and [[Persian carpet|Persian rugs]] that apply the directly proportional [[Ghiordes knot]] in their weaving. The Pazyryk rug is currently displayed at the [[Hermitage Museum]] located in [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], [[Russia]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The World's Oldest Rug: The Pazyryk Rug - Our Blog - Matt Camron Rugs & Tapestries - Antique Oriental Persian Rugs |url=https://www.mattcamron.com/blog/the-worlds-oldest-rug-the-pazyryk-rug |access-date=2023-08-04 |website=www.mattcamron.com |language=en}}</ref>

Digital tools have also aided in making patterns by decreasing the amount of an effect known as "tracking", in which the eye is inadvertently drawn to parts of textiles that expose the discontinuity of the textile and reveal its pattern.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Patterns and Repeats|oclc=866622297}}</ref> These tools, alongside the innovation of digital [[inkjet printing]], have allowed the textile printing process to become faster, more [[scalable]], and more [[sustainable]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Technology for Digital Textile Printing|oclc=866622297}}</ref>

=== Woven textile design ===
Woven textile design originates from the practice of [[weaving]], which produces fabric by interlacing a vertical yarn ([[Warp and weft|warp]]) and a horizontal yarn ([[Warp and weft|weft]]), most often at right angles.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Britannica Concise Encyclopedia |date=2006|publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica|isbn=978-1-84972-210-0|location=Chicago|chapter=Weaving|oclc=436847805}}</ref> Woven textile designs are created by various types of [[loom]]s and are now predominantly produced using a mechanized or computerized [[Jacquard machine|jacquard loom]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Hand Woven Textile Designs|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>[[File:Philbrook_-_Navajo_Satteldecke.jpg|thumb|Woven textile design: A woven [[Navajo]] [[saddle blanket]] from the [[Philbrook Museum of Art|Philbrook Museum]] in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma|Tulsa]], [[Oklahoma]]]]Designs within the context of weaving are created using various types of yarns, using variance in texture, size, and color to construct a stylized patterned or [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] fabric. There is a large range of yarn types available to the designer, including but not limited to [[cotton]], [[twill]], [[linen]], and synthetic fibers. To produce the woven fabric, the designer first delineates and visualizes the sequence of threading, which is traditionally drawn out on graph paper known as point paper.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rothstein |first=Natalie |date=1994 |title=The Victoria and Albert Museum's Textile Collection: Woven Textile Design in Britain 1750 to 1850 |url= |location=New York |publisher=Canopy Books |page= |isbn=9781558598508 |oclc=31203715}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Preparation for Design|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref>

The designer also will choose a weave structure that governs the aesthetic design that will be produced. The most common process is a [[plain weave]], in which the yarns interlace in an alternating, tight formation, producing a strong and flexible multi-use fabric. [[Twill]] weaves, which are also common, alternatively use diagonal lines created by floating the warp or the weft to the left or the right.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Twill Weaves|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref> This process creates a softer fabric favored by designers in the fashion and clothing design industries. Common, recognizable twill styles include patterns like [[Houndstooth]] or [[Herringbone (cloth)|Herringbone]].<ref name=":0" />

Beyond weave structure, [[color]] is another dominant aspect in woven textile design. Typically, designers choose two or more contrasting colors that will be woven into patterns based on a chosen threading sequence. Color is also dependent on the size of the yarn: fine yarns will produce a fabric that may change colors when it receives light from different angles, whereas larger yarns will generally produce a more [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] surface.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Colour and Weave|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref>

=== Mixed media textile design ===
[[File:Kazakh_rug_chain_stitch_embroidery.jpg|thumb|Mixed media textile design: An embroidered [[Kazakhs|Kazakh]], chain stitched rug]]
Mixed media textile designs are produced using [[embroidery]] or other various fabric manipulation processes such as [[pleat]]ing, [[appliqué]], [[quilting]], and [[laser cutting]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Mixed media textile design|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

Embroidery is traditionally performed by hand, applying myriad stitches of thread to construct designs and patterns on the textile surface. Similar to printed textile design, embroidery affords the designer artistic and aesthetic control. Typical stitches include but are not limited to the [[Cross-stitch|cross stitch]], the [[chain stitch]], and [[couching]]. Although industrial and [[Machine embroidery|mechanized embroidery]] has become the standard, hand stitching still remains a fixture for fine arts textiles.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Embroidered Textile Design|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

[[Quilting]] is traditionally used to enhance the insulation and warmth of a textile. It also provides the designer with the opportunity to apply aesthetic properties. Most commonly, [[quilt]]s feature geometric and [[collage]] designs formed from various textiles of different textures and colors. Quilting also frequently employs the use of recycled scrap or [[heirloom]] fabrics.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Fabric Manipulation|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref> Quilts are also often used as a medium for an artist to depict a personal or communal narrative: for example, the [[Hmong people]] have a tradition of creating story quilts or cloths illustrating their experiences with [[immigration]] to the [[United States]] from [[East Asia|Eastern]] and [[Southeast Asia|South-eastern Asia]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.wisc.edu/stitched-tapestry-of-hmong-history-unveiled-at-multicultural-center/|title=Stitched tapestry of Hmong history unveiled at Multicultural Center|last=Gjerde|first=Hearther|date=October 27, 2008|website=University of Wisconsin-Madison}}</ref>

== Environmental impact ==
The practice and industry of textile design present [[environmental concerns]]. From the production of cloth from raw material to dyeing and finishing, and the ultimate disposal of products, each step of the process produces environmental impacts. They have been further exacerbated with the emergence of [[fast fashion]] and other modern industrial practices.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Environmental Concerns|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

Predominantly, these environmental impacts stem from the heavy use of hazardous chemicals involved in the textile creation process which must be properly disposed of. Other considerations involve the amount of waste created by the disposal of textile design products and the reclamation and reuse of [[Recycling|recyclable]] textiles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Calamari|first1=Sage|last2=Hyllegard|first2=Karen H.|date=2016-07-07|title=An exploration of designers' perspectives on human health and environmental impacts of interior textiles|journal=Textiles and Clothing Sustainability|volume=2|issue=1|pages=9|doi=10.1186/s40689-016-0020-7|issn=2197-9936|doi-access=free}}</ref> The [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] reported that over 15 million tons of textile waste is created annually. This consists of some 5% of all [[Municipal solid waste|municipal waste]] generated. Only 15% of that waste is recovered and reused.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/2013_advncng_smm_rpt.pdf|title=Advancing Sustainable Materials Management: Facts and Figures 2013|website=United States Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref>

The existence and awareness of the negative environmental impacts of textile production has resulted in the emergence new technologies and practices. Textile designs involving the use of synthetic dyes and materials can result in harmful effects on the environment. This has caused a shift towards using natural dyes or materials and research towards other mediums that result in less harm to the environment. This research includes testing new ways to collect [[natural resource]]s and how these natural resources work with other materials.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2020-02-01|title=The education of art culture at Sultanate of Oman through the multidisciplinary integration between graphic design and eco-friendly textile printing. Part 1: Standardization of extraction and dyeing with natural wastes products|journal=Energy Reports|language=en|volume=6|pages=933–939|doi=10.1016/j.egyr.2019.12.020|issn=2352-4847|doi-access=free|last1=Mansour |first1=H. |last2=Hilal |first2=N. |last3=Alhajri |first3=S. |last4=Al-Yahyai |first4=F. |last5=Al-Amri |first5=M. |bibcode=2020EnRep...6..933M |hdl=10419/243845 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

[[Electronic textile]]s involve items of clothing with electronic devices or technology woven into the fabric, such as heaters, lights, or sensors. These textiles can potentially have additional harmful environmental effects, such as producing [[electronic waste]]. Because of this, these textiles are often made by manufacturers with sustainability in mind.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Köhler|first=Andreas R.|date=2013-10-01|title=Challenges for eco-design of emerging technologies: The case of electronic textiles|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261306913003270|journal=Materials & Design|language=en|volume=51|pages=51–60|doi=10.1016/j.matdes.2013.04.012|issn=0261-3069|url-access=subscription}}</ref> These new approaches to textile design attempt to lessen the negative environmental impact of these textiles.

These concerns have led to the birth of [[Sustainability|sustainable]] textile design movements and the practice of [[ecological design]] within the field. For instance, London's [[Royal Society of Arts|Royal Society of the Arts]] hosts design competitions that compel all entrants to center their design and manufacturing methods around sustainable practices and materials.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Textile design, the environment, and science|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

== Textile design in different cultures ==
[[File:African Textile Design Pattern.jpg|thumb|Strip-woven textile design: African fabric]]
Textile patterns, designs, weaving methods, and cultural significance vary across the world. African countries use textiles as a form of cultural expression and way of life. They use textiles to liven up the interior of a space or accentuate and decorate the body of an individual. The textile designs of African cultures involve the process of strip-woven fibers that can repeat a pattern or vary from strip to strip.<ref>{{Cite book|last=LaGamma|first=Alisa|title=The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End.|publisher=Metropolitan Museum of Art|year=2009|isbn=9780300149623|location=New York|pages=88–99}}</ref>

== History ==
The history of textile design dates back thousands of years. Due to the decomposition of textile fibers, early examples of textile design are rare. However, some of the oldest known and preserved examples of textiles were discovered in the form of [[Fishing net|nets]] and [[Basket weaving|basketry]], dating from [[Neolithic]] cultures in 5000 BCE. When [[Trade|trade networks]] formed in European countries, textiles like [[silk]], [[wool]], [[cotton]], and [[Flax|flax fibers]] became valuable commodities. Many early cultures including [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]], Chinese, African, and [[Peru]]vian practiced early weaving techniques. One of the oldest examples of textile design was found in an ancient [[Siberia]]n tomb in 1947. The tomb was said to be that of a prince aging back to 464 AD, making the tomb and all of its contents over 2,500 years old. The rug, known as the [[Pazyryk rug]], was preserved inside ice and is detailed with elaborate designs of deer and men riding on horseback. The designs are similar to present-day [[Anatolian rug|Anatolian]] and [[Persian carpet|Persian rugs]] that apply the directly proportional [[Ghiordes knot]] in their weaving. The Pazyryk rug is currently displayed at the [[Hermitage Museum]] located in [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], [[Russia]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The World's Oldest Rug: The Pazyryk Rug - Our Blog - Matt Camron Rugs & Tapestries - Antique Oriental Persian Rugs |url=https://www.mattcamron.com/blog/the-worlds-oldest-rug-the-pazyryk-rug |access-date=2023-08-04 |website=www.mattcamron.com |language=en}}</ref>

Quilting also frequently employs the use of recycled scrap or [[heirloom]] fabrics.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Fabric Manipulation|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref> Quilts are also often used as a medium for an artist to depict a personal or communal narrative: for example, the [[Hmong people]] have a tradition of creating story quilts or cloths illustrating their experiences with [[immigration]] to the [[United States]] from [[East Asia|Eastern]] and [[Southeast Asia|South-eastern Asia]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.wisc.edu/stitched-tapestry-of-hmong-history-unveiled-at-multicultural-center/|title=Stitched tapestry of Hmong history unveiled at Multicultural Center|last=Gjerde|first=Hearther|date=October 27, 2008|website=University of Wisconsin-Madison}}</ref>

== Environmental impact ==
The practice and industry of textile design present [[environmental concerns]]. From the production of cloth from raw material to dyeing and finishing, and the ultimate disposal of products, each step of the process produces environmental impacts. They have been further exacerbated with the emergence of [[fast fashion]] and other modern industrial practices.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Environmental Concerns|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

Predominantly, these environmental impacts stem from the heavy use of hazardous chemicals involved in the textile creation process which must be properly disposed of. Other considerations involve the amount of waste created by the disposal of textile design products and the reclamation and reuse of [[Recycling|recyclable]] textiles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Calamari|first1=Sage|last2=Hyllegard|first2=Karen H.|date=2016-07-07|title=An exploration of designers' perspectives on human health and environmental impacts of interior textiles|journal=Textiles and Clothing Sustainability|volume=2|issue=1|pages=9|doi=10.1186/s40689-016-0020-7|issn=2197-9936|doi-access=free}}</ref> The [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] reported that over 15 million tons of textile waste is created annually. This consists of some 5% of all [[Municipal solid waste|municipal waste]] generated. Only 15% of that waste is recovered and reused.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/2013_advncng_smm_rpt.pdf|title=Advancing Sustainable Materials Management: Facts and Figures 2013|website=United States Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref>

The existence and awareness of the negative environmental impacts of textile production has resulted in the emergence new technologies and practices. Textile designs involving the use of synthetic dyes and materials can result in harmful effects on the environment. This has caused a shift towards using natural dyes or materials and research towards other mediums that result in less harm to the environment. This research includes testing new ways to collect [[natural resource]]s and how these natural resources work with other materials.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2020-02-01|title=The education of art culture at Sultanate of Oman through the multidisciplinary integration between graphic design and eco-friendly textile printing. Part 1: Standardization of extraction and dyeing with natural wastes products|journal=Energy Reports|language=en|volume=6|pages=933–939|doi=10.1016/j.egyr.2019.12.020|issn=2352-4847|doi-access=free|last1=Mansour |first1=H. |last2=Hilal |first2=N. |last3=Alhajri |first3=S. |last4=Al-Yahyai |first4=F. |last5=Al-Amri |first5=M. |bibcode=2020EnRep...6..933M }}</ref>

[[Electronic textile]]s involve items of clothing with electronic devices or technology woven into the fabric, such as heaters, lights, or sensors. These textiles can potentially have additional harmful environmental effects, such as producing [[electronic waste]]. Because of this, these textiles are often made by manufacturers with sustainability in mind.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Köhler|first=Andreas R.|date=2013-10-01|title=Challenges for eco-design of emerging technologies: The case of electronic textiles|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261306913003270|journal=Materials & Design|language=en|volume=51|pages=51–60|doi=10.1016/j.matdes.2013.04.012|issn=0261-3069|url-access=subscription}}</ref> These new approaches to textile design attempt to lessen the negative environmental impact of these textiles.

For instance, London's [[Royal Society of Arts|Royal Society of the Arts]] hosts design competitions that compel all entrants to center their design and manufacturing methods around sustainable practices and materials.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Textile design, the environment, and science|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

== Textile design in different cultures ==
[[File:African Textile Design Pattern.jpg|thumb|Strip-woven textile design: African fabric]]
Textile patterns, designs, weaving methods, and cultural significance vary across the world. African countries use textiles as a form of cultural expression and way of life. They use textiles to liven up the interior of a space or accentuate and decorate the body of an individual. The textile designs of African cultures involve the process of strip-woven fibers that can repeat a pattern or vary from strip to strip.<ref>{{Cite book|last=LaGamma|first=Alisa|title=The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End.|publisher=Metropolitan Museum of Art|year=2009|isbn=9780300149623|location=New York|pages=88–99}}</ref>

== History ==
The history of textile design dates back thousands of years. Due to the decomposition of textile fibers, early examples of textile design are rare. However, some of the oldest known and preserved examples of textiles were discovered in the form of [[Fishing net|nets]] and [[Basket weaving|basketry]], dating from [[Neolithic]] cultures in 5000 BCE. When [[Trade|trade networks]] formed in European countries, textiles like [[silk]], [[wool]], [[cotton]], and [[Flax|flax fibers]] became valuable commodities. Many early cultures including [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]], Chinese, African, and [[Peru]]vian practiced early weaving techniques. One of the oldest examples of textile design was found in an ancient [[Siberia]]n tomb in 1947. The tomb was said to be that of a prince aging back to 464 AD, making the tomb and all of its contents over 2,500 years old. The rug, known as the [[Pazyryk rug]], was preserved inside ice and is detailed with elaborate designs of deer and men riding on horseback. The designs are similar to present-day [[Anatolian rug|Anatolian]] and [[Persian carpet|Persian rugs]] that apply the directly proportional [[Ghiordes knot]] in their weaving. The Pazyryk rug is currently displayed at the [[Hermitage Museum]] located in [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], [[Russia]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The World's Oldest Rug: The Pazyryk Rug - Our Blog - Matt Camron Rugs & Tapestries - Antique Oriental Persian Rugs |url=https://www.mattcamron.com/blog/the-worlds-oldest-rug-the-pazyryk-rug |access-date=2023-08-04 |website=www.mattcamron.com |language=en}}</ref>

== Overview ==
Articles produced using textile design include [[clothing]], [[carpet]]s, [[Drapery|drapes]], and [[towel]]s.<ref name="Collier, Bide and Tortora">{{cite book |last1=Collier |first1=Billie J. |last2=Bide |first2=Martin J. |last3=Tortora |first3=Phyllis G.|title=Understanding of Textiles |url= |publisher=Pearson Prentice Hall |year=2009|location=Upper Saddle River, New Jersey |edition=7th |isbn=978-0-13-118770-2 |oclc=212376154}}</ref> Textile design requires an understanding of the technical aspects of [[textile manufacturing|the production process]], as well as the properties of numerous [[fiber]]s, [[yarn]]s, and [[dye]]s.<ref name="Gale">{{cite book |last1=Gale |first1=Colin |last2=Kaur |first2=Jasbir |date=2002 |title=The Textile Book |url= |location=Oxford |publisher=Berg |page=37 |isbn=1-85973-512-6 |oclc=48516971}}</ref>

== Textile design disciplines ==

=== Printed textile design ===
[[File:Textile,_Strawberry_Thief,_designed_1883,_printed_ca._1934_(CH_18340065).jpg|thumb|Printed textile design: [[William Morris]], [[Strawberry Thief (William Morris)|Strawberry Thief]], 1883<ref>{{Cite book|last=Parry |first=Linda |title=William Morris Textiles|date=1983 |location=New York |publisher=Viking Press|isbn=0-670-77075-2|oclc=8221337}}</ref>]]
Printed textile designs are created by using various printing techniques on fabric, cloth, and other materials. Printed textile designers are mainly involved in designing patterns for home interior products like carpets, wallpapers, and ceramics. They also work in the [[Fashion industry|fashion and clothing industries]], the [[Pulp and paper industry|paper industry]], and in designing stationery and [[Gift wrapping|gift wrap]].<ref>{{Citation|title=The framework|date=2011|url=https://www.bloomsburyappliedvisualarts.com/encyclopedia-chapter?docid=b-9781474218535&tocid=b-9781474218535-chapter1|work=The Fundamentals of Printed Textile Design|pages=8–43|publisher=AVA Publishing SA Distributed by Thames & Hudson (ex-North America) Distributed in the USA & Canada by: English Language Support Office|language=en|doi=10.5040/9781474218535.ch-001|isbn=978-1-4742-1853-5|access-date=2020-04-17}}</ref>

There are numerous established printed styles and designs that can be broken down into four major categories: floral, geometric, world cultures, and conversational.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last=Briggs-Goode |first=Amanda |title=Printed Textile Design |isbn=978-1-78067-403-2 |location=London |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Design in Context |oclc=898176484}}</ref> [[Floral design]]s include flowers, plants, or other botanical elements. [[Geometric design]]s feature elements, both inorganic and [[Abstract art|abstract]], such as [[tessellation]]s. World culture designs may be traced to a specific geographic, ethnic, or anthropological source. Finally, conversational designs are designs that fit less easily into the other categories; they may be described as presenting "imagery that references popular icons of a particular period or season, or which is unique and challenges our perceptions in some way."<ref name=":22" /> Each category contains subcategories, which include more specific individual styles and designs.<ref name=":22" />

Moreover, different fabrics, like [[silk]] and [[wool]], require different types of dye. Other protein-based fabrics require acidic dyes, whereas [[Synthetic fiber|synthetic fabrics]] require specialized [[disperse dye|dispersed dye]]s.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-78539-200-9 |location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Screen-printed textile designs |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

The advent of [[computer-aided design]] [[software]], such as [[Adobe Photoshop]] and [[Adobe Illustrator|Illustrator]], has allowed each discipline of textile design to evolve and innovate new practices and processes but has most influenced the production of printed textile designs.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London|chapter=Introduction|oclc=866622297}}</ref> Digital tools have influenced the process of creating repeating patterns or motifs, or repeats. Repeats are used to create patterns both visible and invisible to the eye: geometric patterns are intended to depict clear, intentional patterns, whereas floral or organic designs are intended to create unbroken repeats that are ideally undetectable. Digital tools have also aided in making patterns by decreasing the amount of an effect known as "tracking", in which the eye is inadvertently drawn to parts of textiles that expose the discontinuity of the textile and reveal its pattern.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Patterns and Repeats|oclc=866622297}}</ref> These tools, alongside the innovation of digital [[inkjet printing]], have allowed the textile printing process to become faster, more [[scalable]], and more [[sustainable]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Technology for Digital Textile Printing|oclc=866622297}}</ref>

=== Woven textile design ===
Woven textile design originates from the practice of [[weaving]], which produces fabric by interlacing a vertical yarn ([[Warp and weft|warp]]) and a horizontal yarn ([[Warp and weft|weft]]), most often at right angles.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Britannica Concise Encyclopedia |date=2006|publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica|isbn=978-1-84972-210-0|location=Chicago|chapter=Weaving|oclc=436847805}}</ref> Woven textile designs are created by various types of [[loom]]s and are now predominantly produced using a mechanized or computerized [[Jacquard machine|jacquard loom]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Hand Woven Textile Designs|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>[[File:Philbrook_-_Navajo_Satteldecke.jpg|thumb|Woven textile design: A woven [[Navajo]] [[saddle blanket]] from the [[Philbrook Museum of Art|Philbrook Museum]] in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma|Tulsa]], [[Oklahoma]]]]Designs within the context of weaving are created using various types of yarns, using variance in texture, size, and color to construct a stylized patterned or [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] fabric. There is a large range of yarn types available to the designer, including but not limited to [[cotton]], [[twill]], [[linen]], and synthetic fibers. To produce the woven fabric, the designer first delineates and visualizes the sequence of threading, which is traditionally drawn out on graph paper known as point paper.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rothstein |first=Natalie |date=1994 |title=The Victoria and Albert Museum's Textile Collection: Woven Textile Design in Britain 1750 to 1850 |url= |location=New York |publisher=Canopy Books |page= |isbn=9781558598508 |oclc=31203715}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Preparation for Design|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref>

The designer also will choose a weave structure that governs the aesthetic design that will be produced. The most common process is a [[plain weave]], in which the yarns interlace in an alternating, tight formation, producing a strong and flexible multi-use fabric. [[Twill]] weaves, which are also common, alternatively use diagonal lines created by floating the warp or the weft to the left or the right.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Twill Weaves|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref> This process creates a softer fabric favored by designers in the fashion and clothing design industries. Common, recognizable twill styles include patterns like [[Houndstooth]] or [[Herringbone (cloth)|Herringbone]].<ref name=":0" />

Beyond weave structure, [[color]] is another dominant aspect in woven textile design. Typically, designers choose two or more contrasting colors that will be woven into patterns based on a chosen threading sequence. Color is also dependent on the size of the yarn: fine yarns will produce a fabric that may change colors when it receives light from different angles, whereas larger yarns will generally produce a more [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] surface.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Colour and Weave|date=28 April 2014 |oclc=884590266}}</ref>

== Overview ==
Articles produced using textile design include [[clothing]], [[carpet]]s, [[Drapery|drapes]], and [[towel]]s.<ref name="Collier, Bide and Tortora">{{cite book |last1=Collier |first1=Billie J. |last2=Bide |first2=Martin J. |last3=Tortora |first3=Phyllis G.|title=Understanding of Textiles |url= |publisher=Pearson Prentice Hall |year=2009|location=Upper Saddle River, New Jersey |edition=7th |isbn=978-0-13-118770-2 |oclc=212376154}}</ref> Textile design requires an understanding of the technical aspects of [[textile manufacturing|the production process]], as well as the properties of numerous [[fiber]]s, [[yarn]]s, and [[dye]]s.<ref name="Gale">{{cite book |last1=Gale |first1=Colin |last2=Kaur |first2=Jasbir |date=2002 |title=The Textile Book |url= |location=Oxford |publisher=Berg |page=37 |isbn=1-85973-512-6 |oclc=48516971}}</ref>

== Textile design disciplines ==

=== Printed textile design ===
[[File:Textile,_Strawberry_Thief,_designed_1883,_printed_ca._1934_(CH_18340065).jpg|thumb|Printed textile design: [[William Morris]], [[Strawberry Thief (William Morris)|Strawberry Thief]], 1883<ref>{{Cite book|last=Parry |first=Linda |title=William Morris Textiles|date=1983 |location=New York |publisher=Viking Press|isbn=0-670-77075-2|oclc=8221337}}</ref>]]
Printed textile designs are created by using various printing techniques on fabric, cloth, and other materials. Printed textile designers are mainly involved in designing patterns for home interior products like carpets, wallpapers, and ceramics. They also work in the [[Fashion industry|fashion and clothing industries]], the [[Pulp and paper industry|paper industry]], and in designing stationery and [[Gift wrapping|gift wrap]].<ref>{{Citation|title=The framework|date=2011|url=https://www.bloomsburyappliedvisualarts.com/encyclopedia-chapter?docid=b-9781474218535&tocid=b-9781474218535-chapter1|work=The Fundamentals of Printed Textile Design|pages=8–43|publisher=AVA Publishing SA Distributed by Thames & Hudson (ex-North America) Distributed in the USA & Canada by: English Language Support Office|language=en|doi=10.5040/9781474218535.ch-001|isbn=978-1-4742-1853-5|access-date=2020-04-17}}</ref>

There are numerous established printed styles and designs that can be broken down into four major categories: floral, geometric, world cultures, and conversational.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last=Briggs-Goode |first=Amanda |title=Printed Textile Design |isbn=978-1-78067-403-2 |location=London |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Design in Context |oclc=898176484}}</ref> [[Floral design]]s include flowers, plants, or other botanical elements. [[Geometric design]]s feature elements, both inorganic and [[Abstract art|abstract]], such as [[tessellation]]s. World culture designs may be traced to a specific geographic, ethnic, or anthropological source. Finally, conversational designs are designs that fit less easily into the other categories; they may be described as presenting "imagery that references popular icons of a particular period or season, or which is unique and challenges our perceptions in some way."<ref name=":22" /> Each category contains subcategories, which include more specific individual styles and designs.<ref name=":22" />

Moreover, different fabrics, like [[silk]] and [[wool]], require different types of dye. Other protein-based fabrics require acidic dyes, whereas [[Synthetic fiber|synthetic fabrics]] require specialized [[disperse dye|dispersed dye]]s.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-78539-200-9 |location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Screen-printed textile designs |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

The advent of [[computer-aided design]] [[software]], such as [[Adobe Photoshop]] and [[Adobe Illustrator|Illustrator]], has allowed each discipline of textile design to evolve and innovate new practices and processes but has most influenced the production of printed textile designs.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London|chapter=Introduction|oclc=866622297}}</ref> Digital tools have influenced the process of creating repeating patterns or motifs, or repeats. Repeats are used to create patterns both visible and invisible to the eye: geometric patterns are intended to depict clear, intentional patterns, whereas floral or organic designs are intended to create unbroken repeats that are ideally undetectable. Digital tools have also aided in making patterns by decreasing the amount of an effect known as "tracking", in which the eye is inadvertently drawn to parts of textiles that expose the discontinuity of the textile and reveal its pattern.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Patterns and Repeats|oclc=866622297}}</ref> These tools, alongside the innovation of digital [[inkjet printing]], have allowed the textile printing process to become faster, more [[scalable]], and more [[sustainable]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bowles |first1=Melanie |last2=Isaac |first2=Ceri |title=Digital Textile Design|date=2012|publisher=Laurence King|isbn=978-1-78067-223-6|edition=2nd|location=London |chapter=Technology for Digital Textile Printing|oclc=866622297}}</ref>

=== Woven textile design ===
Woven textile design originates from the practice of [[weaving]], which produces fabric by interlacing a vertical yarn ([[Warp and weft|warp]]) and a horizontal yarn ([[Warp and weft|weft]]), most often at right angles.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Britannica Concise Encyclopedia |date=2006|publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica|isbn=978-1-84972-210-0|location=Chicago|chapter=Weaving|oclc=436847805}}</ref> Woven textile designs are created by various types of [[loom]]s and are now predominantly produced using a mechanized or computerized [[Jacquard machine|jacquard loom]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Hand Woven Textile Designs|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>[[File:Philbrook_-_Navajo_Satteldecke.jpg|thumb|Woven textile design: A woven [[Navajo]] [[saddle blanket]] from the [[Philbrook Museum of Art|Philbrook Museum]] in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma|Tulsa]], [[Oklahoma]]]]Designs within the context of weaving are created using various types of yarns, using variance in texture, size, and color to construct a stylized patterned or [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] fabric. There is a large range of yarn types available to the designer, including but not limited to [[cotton]], [[twill]], [[linen]], and synthetic fibers. To produce the woven fabric, the designer first delineates and visualizes the sequence of threading, which is traditionally drawn out on graph paper known as point paper.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rothstein |first=Natalie |date=1994 |title=The Victoria and Albert Museum's Textile Collection: Woven Textile Design in Britain 1750 to 1850 |url= |location=New York |publisher=Canopy Books |page= |isbn=9781558598508 |oclc=31203715}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Preparation for Design|oclc=884590266}}</ref>

The designer also will choose a weave structure that governs the aesthetic design that will be produced. The most common process is a [[plain weave]], in which the yarns interlace in an alternating, tight formation, producing a strong and flexible multi-use fabric. [[Twill]] weaves, which are also common, alternatively use diagonal lines created by floating the warp or the weft to the left or the right.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Twill Weaves|oclc=884590266}}</ref> This process creates a softer fabric favored by designers in the fashion and clothing design industries. Common, recognizable twill styles include patterns like [[Houndstooth]] or [[Herringbone (cloth)|Herringbone]].<ref name=":0" />

Beyond weave structure, [[color]] is another dominant aspect in woven textile design. Typically, designers choose two or more contrasting colors that will be woven into patterns based on a chosen threading sequence. Color is also dependent on the size of the yarn: fine yarns will produce a fabric that may change colors when it receives light from different angles, whereas larger yarns will generally produce a more [[Monochrome|monochromatic]] surface.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Shenton, Jan|title=Woven textile design|others=Ridsdale, Eleanor|isbn=978-1-78067-569-5|location=London [England]|chapter=Colour and Weave|oclc=884590266}}</ref>

=== Mixed media textile design ===
[[File:Kazakh_rug_chain_stitch_embroidery.jpg|thumb|Mixed media textile design: An embroidered [[Kazakhs|Kazakh]], chain stitched rug]]
Mixed media textile designs are produced using [[embroidery]] or other various fabric manipulation processes such as [[pleat]]ing, [[appliqué]], [[quilting]], and [[laser cutting]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Mixed media textile design|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

Embroidery is traditionally performed by hand, applying myriad stitches of thread to construct designs and patterns on the textile surface. Similar to printed textile design, embroidery affords the designer artistic and aesthetic control. Typical stitches include but are not limited to the [[Cross-stitch|cross stitch]], the [[chain stitch]], and [[couching]]. Although industrial and [[Machine embroidery|mechanized embroidery]] has become the standard, hand stitching still remains a fixture for fine arts textiles.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Embroidered Textile Design|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

[[Quilting]] is traditionally used to enhance the insulation and warmth of a textile. It also provides the designer with the opportunity to apply aesthetic properties. Most commonly, [[quilt]]s feature geometric and [[collage]] designs formed from various textiles of different textures and colors. Quilting also frequently employs the use of recycled scrap or [[heirloom]] fabrics.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England] |publisher=Laurence King |chapter=Fabric Manipulation|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref> Quilts are also often used as a medium for an artist to depict a personal or communal narrative: for example, the [[Hmong people]] have a tradition of creating story quilts or cloths illustrating their experiences with [[immigration]] to the [[United States]] from [[East Asia|Eastern]] and [[Southeast Asia|South-eastern Asia]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.wisc.edu/stitched-tapestry-of-hmong-history-unveiled-at-multicultural-center/|title=Stitched tapestry of Hmong history unveiled at Multicultural Center|last=Gjerde|first=Hearther|date=October 27, 2008|website=University of Wisconsin-Madison}}</ref>

== Environmental impact ==
The practice and industry of textile design present [[environmental concerns]]. From the production of cloth from raw material to dyeing and finishing, and the ultimate disposal of products, each step of the process produces environmental impacts. They have been further exacerbated with the emergence of [[fast fashion]] and other modern industrial practices.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Environmental Concerns|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

Predominantly, these environmental impacts stem from the heavy use of hazardous chemicals involved in the textile creation process which must be properly disposed of. Other considerations involve the amount of waste created by the disposal of textile design products and the reclamation and reuse of [[Recycling|recyclable]] textiles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Calamari|first1=Sage|last2=Hyllegard|first2=Karen H.|date=2016-07-07|title=An exploration of designers' perspectives on human health and environmental impacts of interior textiles|journal=Textiles and Clothing Sustainability|volume=2|issue=1|pages=9|doi=10.1186/s40689-016-0020-7|issn=2197-9936|doi-access=free}}</ref> The [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] reported that over 15 million tons of textile waste is created annually. This consists of some 5% of all [[Municipal solid waste|municipal waste]] generated. Only 15% of that waste is recovered and reused.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/2013_advncng_smm_rpt.pdf|title=Advancing Sustainable Materials Management: Facts and Figures 2013|website=United States Environmental Protection Agency}}</ref>

The existence and awareness of the negative environmental impacts of textile production has resulted in the emergence new technologies and practices. Textile designs involving the use of synthetic dyes and materials can result in harmful effects on the environment. This has caused a shift towards using natural dyes or materials and research towards other mediums that result in less harm to the environment. This research includes testing new ways to collect [[natural resource]]s and how these natural resources work with other materials.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2020-02-01|title=The education of art culture at Sultanate of Oman through the multidisciplinary integration between graphic design and eco-friendly textile printing. Part 1: Standardization of extraction and dyeing with natural wastes products|journal=Energy Reports|language=en|volume=6|pages=933–939|doi=10.1016/j.egyr.2019.12.020|issn=2352-4847|doi-access=free|last1=Mansour |first1=H. |last2=Hilal |first2=N. |last3=Alhajri |first3=S. |last4=Al-Yahyai |first4=F. |last5=Al-Amri |first5=M. |bibcode=2020EnRep...6..933M }}</ref>

[[Electronic textile]]s involve items of clothing with electronic devices or technology woven into the fabric, such as heaters, lights, or sensors. These textiles can potentially have additional harmful environmental effects, such as producing [[electronic waste]]. Because of this, these textiles are often made by manufacturers with sustainability in mind.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Köhler|first=Andreas R.|date=2013-10-01|title=Challenges for eco-design of emerging technologies: The case of electronic textiles|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261306913003270|journal=Materials & Design|language=en|volume=51|pages=51–60|doi=10.1016/j.matdes.2013.04.012|issn=0261-3069}}</ref> These new approaches to textile design attempt to lessen the negative environmental impact of these textiles.

These concerns have led to the birth of [[Sustainability|sustainable]] textile design movements and the practice of [[ecological design]] within the field. For instance, London's [[Royal Society of Arts|Royal Society of the Arts]] hosts design competitions that compel all entrants to center their design and manufacturing methods around sustainable practices and materials.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke |first=Simon |title=Textile Design|isbn=978-1-78539-200-9|location=London [England]|publisher=Laurence King|chapter=Textile design, the environment, and science|year=2011 |oclc=908338301}}</ref>

== Textile design in different cultures ==
[[File:African Textile Design Pattern.jpg|thumb|Strip-woven textile design: African fabric]]
Textile patterns, designs, weaving methods, and cultural significance vary across the world. African countries use textiles as a form of cultural expression and way of life. They use textiles to liven up the interior of a space or accentuate and decorate the body of an individual. The textile designs of African cultures involve the process of strip-woven fibers that can repeat a pattern or vary from strip to strip.<ref>{{Cite book|last=LaGamma|first=Alisa|title=The Essential Art of African Textiles: Design Without End.|publisher=Metropolitan Museum of Art|year=2009|isbn=9780300149623|location=New York|pages=88–99}}</ref>

== History ==
The history of textile design dates back thousands of years. Due to the decomposition of textile fibers, early examples of textile design are rare. However, some of the oldest known and preserved examples of textiles were discovered in the form of [[Fishing net|nets]] and [[Basket weaving|basketry]], dating from [[Neolithic]] cultures in 5000 BCE. When [[Trade|trade networks]] formed in European countries, textiles like [[silk]], [[wool]], [[cotton]], and [[Flax|flax fibers]] became valuable commodities. Many early cultures including [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]], Chinese, African, and [[Peru]]vian practiced early weaving techniques. One of the oldest examples of textile design was found in an ancient [[Siberia]]n tomb in 1947. The tomb was said to be that of a prince aging back to 464 AD, making the tomb and all of its contents over 2,500 years old. The rug, known as the [[Pazyryk rug]], was preserved inside ice and is detailed with elaborate designs of deer and men riding on horseback. The designs are similar to present-day [[Anatolian rug|Anatolian]] and [[Persian carpet|Persian rugs]] that apply the directly proportional [[Ghiordes knot]] in their weaving. The Pazyryk rug is currently displayed at the [[Hermitage Museum]] located in [[Saint Petersburg|St. Petersburg]], [[Russia]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The World's Oldest Rug: The Pazyryk Rug - Our Blog - Matt Camron Rugs & Tapestries - Antique Oriental Persian Rugs |url=https://www.mattcamron.com/blog/the-worlds-oldest-rug-the-pazyryk-rug |access-date=2023-08-04 |website=www.mattcamron.com |language=en}}</ref>
